The early life stages of the Bronze featherback (Notopterus notopterus) begin with the emergence of a prolarva from the fertilised egg. Following chorion rupture, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva is remarkably small, measuring only 0.39 cm  in total length at hatch. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of development. The duration of the embryonic period depends strongly on ambient temperature; for instance, the age at hatch has been estimated at approximately 7.83 days  when eggs are incubated at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This short pre-larval phase is followed by the onset of exogenous feeding, where the mouth opens and the larva begins to capture its first prey. The transition to active feeding marks a critical developmental milestone, after which growth accelerates rapidly. The total length at birth, defined as the size of the newly emerged free-swimming individual, is 1.62 cm [Lb = 1.62 cm], a value that reflects the relatively advanced state of the larva at the moment it becomes fully independent of the egg envelope. These early developmental parameters are essential for understanding the species' recruitment dynamics in its riverine habitats.

As the juvenile fish grows, it undergoes a prolonged period of somatic development before reaching reproductive maturity. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies indicate that the ultimate total length attained by this species is 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], though individuals in suboptimal environments often fall short of this maximum. Among the Notopteridae, this size is moderate, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances early maturation with continued growth. The total length at puberty, which marks the initiation of gonadal recrudescence and the onset of vitellogenesis in females, is 27.5 cm [Lp = 27.5 cm]. This size threshold is typically reached after a substantial period of juvenile growth. Data from captive populations maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] show that the age at which females first become reproductively active, corresponding to the first spawning event, is approximately 915 days after hatching [tR = approximately 915 days after hatching]. This relatively late age at first reproduction is consistent with the species' iteroparous breeding pattern and its investment in achieving a moderate body size before allocating resources to egg production.

Reproductive output in Bronze featherback is tightly linked to female body size and environmental temperature. Controlled aquarium studies conducted at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have provided detailed estimates of fecundity and spawning frequency. Females produce approximately 220 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 220 eggs per spawning event] under optimal conditions, with one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year], representing the maximum reproductive rate achievable for this species. This annual fecundity integrates both the modest clutch sizes and the extended intervals between successive spawning events characteristic of notopterids. For a female measuring 23.7 cm in total length, the wet weight recorded is 130 g , providing a useful morphometric relationship linking length to mass that facilitates field-based estimates of condition factor. The gonadosomatic index in gravid individuals can exceed 12%, indicating substantial investment in ovarian tissue during the breeding season. These reproductive parameters, combined with the species' protracted spawning season, contribute to a total annual fecundity that, while not exceptionally high, ensures recruitment across variable environmental conditions.

Longevity and aging patterns in Notopterus notopterus have been assessed through both mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination. The maximum lifespan for this species, representing the oldest documented individual in the wild, is approximately 10,950 days [am = approximately 10,950 days] under the thermal regime typical of its tropical freshwater habitats, where average annual water temperatures hover around 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly 30 years, is notably long for a teleost fish of this body size and suggests a slow pace of life with delayed senescence. The age at birth, defined as the time elapsed between fertilization and the emergence of the free-swimming larva, is 17 days [ab = 17 days] when embryos develop at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This rapid embryonic development, combined with the extended adult lifespan, creates a life-history pattern where the pre-reproductive period constitutes a relatively small fraction of the total life span, allowing many years of repeated spawning once maturity is attained.

Ecologically, the Bronze featherback occupies slow-flowing rivers, oxbow lakes, and floodplain swamps where it is an important component of the ichthyofauna. The species is a nocturnal predator, feeding primarily on insects, crustaceans, and smaller fish. Its laterally compressed body and undulating ribbon-like fin provide exceptional maneuverability in densely vegetated habitats. Comparative analyses within the Notopteridae reveal that N. notopterus exhibits a relatively conservative growth trajectory, with the total length at puberty of 27.5 cm [Lp = 27.5 cm] representing about 46% of the ultimate total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm]. This proportion is typical for iteroparous freshwater fishes that continue somatic growth after reproducing. The wet weight measurement of 130 g  at a total length of 23.7 cm provides a useful reference point for estimating biomass in population surveys. Conservation assessments in parts of its range have noted declines due to habitat degradation and overfishing, underscoring the importance of life-history data for informing sustainable management of this culturally and economically valuable species.
